title: Gender Equality
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the long struggle for gender equality -- four waves of feminism, the persistent pay gap, and why it concerns men as well as women.
competenceGoals: analyze the development of gender equality in English-speaking countries and globally
discuss the ongoing challenges to gender equality including the pay gap, representation, and gender-based violence
reflect on intersectional perspectives on gender and how gender interacts with other social categories

content.content:
## A century of change, and an unfinished journey

A little over a hundred years ago, women in most countries could not vote, own property on equal terms, or pursue many professions. Today, in much of the English-speaking world, women outnumber men in higher education and the law guarantees equality. That is an extraordinary transformation -- and yet gender inequality persists, in different forms, in virtually every society on earth. **Gender equality** -- the principle that all people should have equal rights, opportunities and treatment regardless of gender -- is one of the defining social issues of modern history.

The story is often told in four waves. *First-wave feminism* (mid-1800s to the 1920s) focused on legal rights, above all the vote, beginning symbolically with the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention and winning suffrage in New Zealand (1893), Australia (1902), the UK (1918/1928) and the US (1920). *Second-wave feminism* (1960s-1980s) widened the agenda to workplace discrimination, reproductive rights and domestic violence, captured in the slogan "the personal is political." *Third-wave feminism* (1990s-2000s) embraced diversity, questioned whether the movement had centred too narrowly on white, middle-class women, and introduced intersectionality. *Fourth-wave feminism* (2010s-present) is marked by digital activism, #MeToo, and a global, inclusive scope attentive to transgender and non-binary experiences.

## The key ideas, and the puzzle of the pay gap

A handful of concepts unlock these debates. **Gender equality** means equal rights and opportunities; **gender equity** means fairness in treatment based on respective needs, which may involve treating genders differently to achieve equal outcomes -- parental-leave policies are an example. **Feminism** is not a single ideology but a range of movements sharing the goal of gender equality. **Patriarchy** describes a social system in which men hold primary power across leadership, authority and property -- analysed as a structural feature of society, not merely the attitudes of individual men. The **glass ceiling** is the invisible barrier that stops women advancing beyond a certain level despite their qualifications. **Intersectionality**, a concept developed by legal scholar Kimberle Crenshaw in 1989, argues that different forms of discrimination -- by gender, race, class, sexuality, disability -- intersect and compound, so a Black woman's experience differs from a white woman's. And **toxic masculinity** names cultural norms of male dominance and emotional suppression that harm both men and women.

The **gender pay gap** brings these ideas down to earth. The numbers are real: women earn roughly 82 cents to the dollar in the US, with a gap of about 14.3 percent in the UK, 13.3 percent in Australia and 11.5 percent in Norway -- lower than most, but still there. Crucially, the gap has several distinct causes, and a fair analysis names them all. *Occupational segregation* means women and men cluster in different jobs, with female-dominated fields like care work typically paid less. The *motherhood penalty* sees women's earnings drop after having children while men's do not, reflecting both discrimination and the unequal division of unpaid care. *Negotiation differences*, shaped by gender norms rather than ability, mean women are less likely to negotiate -- and may be penalised socially when they do. *Direct discrimination* persists despite being illegal, and *part-time work*, often tied to caregiving, pays less per hour. The gap also has an intersectional dimension: in the US, Black women earn about 67 cents and Latina women about 57 cents to a white man's dollar, as gender and race compound.

questions.task: Who developed the concept of intersectionality in 1989?
questions.solution: Legal scholar Kimberle Crenshaw developed the concept of intersectionality in 1989, describing how different forms of discrimination compound.

A law banning mothers from working

To analyse the issue fairly and show it has multiple causes

content.content:
## Progress, remaining gaps, and the men in the story

It is important to recognise genuine progress. In most English-speaking countries women now outnumber men in higher education and earn the majority of degrees; anti-discrimination laws exist everywhere; women's representation in politics and business has risen; and attitudes toward gender roles have shifted markedly. But significant challenges remain, and naming them is part of an honest account. In politics, women hold roughly 28 percent of seats in the US Congress, 35 percent in the UK Parliament and 45 percent in the Norwegian Parliament -- only the Nordic countries approach parity. In business, women hold only about ten percent of Fortune 500 CEO positions. Gender-based violence remains pervasive, with an estimated one in three women worldwide experiencing physical or sexual violence. Women perform around 75 percent of the world's unpaid care work, essential labour that is uncounted in GDP. And reproductive rights remain contested, as the US Supreme Court's 2022 overturning of *Roe v. Wade* showed.

A balanced treatment also recognises that gender equality is not only about women. Men face higher rates of suicide, workplace death, incarceration and homelessness, and traditional masculinity norms discourage them from seeking help for mental-health problems. A complete picture includes these realities rather than ignoring them. Norway and the other Nordic countries are often held up as leaders precisely because they take a *structural* approach: generous parental leave with a "father's quota" encouraging men to take time off, subsidised childcare, gender quotas requiring 40 percent female representation on corporate boards, strong legal protections, and a culture of shared parenting. These policies suggest that equality advances furthest not through attitudes alone but through changing the structures within which everyone lives and works.

exercise.task: Test yourself on progress and remaining challenges:

questions.task: Roughly what share of Fortune 500 CEO positions do women hold?
questions.solution: Women hold only about 10 percent of CEO positions in Fortune 500 companies, illustrating that the glass ceiling remains intact at the top.

questions.task: Why does the chapter say gender equality is not only a women's issue?

options.text: Because men face no gender-specific challenges
Because men face higher rates of suicide, workplace death and homelessness, and stigma around seeking help
Because women have full equality already

questions.solution: A balanced account notes that men face gender-specific challenges, including higher rates of suicide, workplace death, incarceration and homelessness, partly due to rigid masculinity norms.

questions.task: What is distinctive about the Nordic approach to gender equality?

options.text: It relies only on changing attitudes
It is structural, using policies like parental leave, childcare and board quotas

questions.solution: The Nordic model takes a structural approach, with father's-quota parental leave, subsidised childcare, board gender quotas and strong legal protections.

questions.task: Approximately how much of the world's unpaid care work do women perform?
questions.solution: Women perform approximately 75 percent of the world's unpaid care work -- childcare, elder care, cooking and cleaning -- which is essential but uncounted in GDP.

content.content:
## In short

The struggle for gender equality has moved through four waves, each widening the agenda from the vote to workplace rights, to diversity and intersectionality, to today's digital, global activism. Genuine progress has come in education, law and culture, yet challenges persist: the gender pay gap (with its multiple causes), the glass ceiling, gender-based violence and the vast burden of unpaid care work. Intersectionality shows that gender inequality is experienced differently across race, class and other categories, and a fair account recognises that men, too, face gender-specific challenges. The Nordic countries demonstrate that structural policies -- parental leave, childcare, quotas -- can move equality furthest, because changing structures, not just attitudes, is what lasts.
